property_summary: For every nonzero amount passed to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference contract sets betLimit equal to that amount (i.e., betLimit becomes exactly amount when initial betLimit is 0), whereas the mutant increases the existing betLimit by amount so betLimit differs for some inputs.

For any nonnegative amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on a freshly deployed contract with initial betLimit 0 results in betLimit == amount (reference); the mutant instead yields betLimit == previous + amount, so for some amount (any nonzero) the observed betLimit differs.

For any nonnegative amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) when the contract's current betLimit is X results in betLimit == X + amount in the mutant but in the reference the intended general rule is: when the reference is freshly deployed with initial betLimit 0, after calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) betLimit == amount; the mutant violates this for some amounts (nonzero) because it adds to the previous betLimit rather than setting it.

For any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on a freshly deployed contract with initial betLimit 0 makes betLimit equal to amount in the reference; the mutant that adds to betLimit instead produces a different betLimit for some amounts (nonzero).

For any uint256 delta, when C is freshly deployed with betLimit = 0, calling AdjustBetAmounts(delta) results in betLimit == delta (reference); the mutant that adds to betLimit instead can make betLimit != delta for some delta (any nonzero), so the property is violated.

For every nonzero uint256 amount passed to AdjustBetAmounts by the owner, the contract sets betLimit equal to the provided amount (reference); the mutant incorrectly sets betLimit to amount/2 for some inputs, so there exist amounts where c.currentBetLimit() != amount after the call.

For any non-negative uint256 amount passed by the owner to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference contract sets betLimit equal to the provided amount; the mutant sets it to amount/2 for some amounts (e.g., odd or any amount where amount/2 != amount), violating this property.

For every uint256 amount passed by the owner to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference contract will make c.currentBetLimit() equal to the exact provided amount after the call; the mutant sometimes sets it to half that amount (amount/2), so there exist fuzzed amounts where c.currentBetLimit() != amount and the property is violated.

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount passed to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference sets betLimit to exactly the provided amount (so c.currentBetLimit() == amount after the call); the mutant sets betLimit = amount/2 for some amounts, so there exist fuzzed amounts where c.currentBetLimit() != amount.

For every uint256 amount and when called by the owner, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on the reference contract makes c.currentBetLimit() equal to the provided amount; the mutant sometimes sets betLimit to amount/2, so there exist fuzzed amounts where c.currentBetLimit() != amount (the test will detect such a divergence by fuzzing amount and checking equality).

For all callers, when AdjustBetAmounts(amount) is invoked by the contract owner (the deployer), betLimit is set to amount; the mutant changes the owner check to whale so calls by the deployer will no longer succeed and the betLimit will not be updated for some inputs (calls from owner).

For any caller address A and uint256 newLimit, if A is the contract owner (the deployer) then calling AdjustBetAmounts(newLimit) always updates c.currentBetLimit() to newLimit in the reference; the mutant that requires whale instead of owner prevents owner callers from updating betLimit for some inputs (owner vs whale), so there exist inputs where c.currentBetLimit() differs after the call.

For every caller address A and value newLimit, if A is the contract owner (the deployer) then calling AdjustBetAmounts(newLimit) always sets c.currentBetLimit() == newLimit; the mutant that checks whale instead of owner can reject deployer calls and thus leaves betLimit unchanged for some inputs (deployer caller), violating the rule.

For every caller address A and newLimit value, if A is the contract owner (the deployer), then calling AdjustBetAmounts(newLimit) succeeds and c.currentBetLimit() equals newLimit; the mutant which requires msg.sender == whale breaks this because calls from the deployer (owner) may be rejected or ignored, leaving betLimit unchanged.

For every caller address A and uint256 newLimit, if A is the contract owner (the deploying address), then calling AdjustBetAmounts(newLimit) always succeeds and sets c.currentBetLimit() == newLimit; the mutant that replaces the owner check with msg.sender == whale prevents the deploying owner from changing betLimit for some inputs (owner-calls), so the mutant leaves c.currentBetLimit() != newLimit for those inputs.

For any input amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on the reference contract sets betLimit exactly to amount (no implicit clamping); the mutant clamps amounts above 1 ether to 1 ether and thus will produce a different betLimit for amounts > 1 ether.

For any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on the reference contract sets betLimit equal to amount (no clamping), whereas the mutant clamps amounts greater than 1 ether so for some inputs (amount > 1 ether) the resulting betLimit differs.

For every uint256 amount the reference contract sets betLimit exactly to the provided amount when AdjustBetAmounts is called by the owner; the mutant clamps values above 1 ether to 1 ether, so for some amounts > 1 ether the stored betLimit will not equal the provided amount.

For any uint256 amount, when the owner calls AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the contract's betLimit equals the provided amount; the mutant clamps amounts above 1 ether so for some amounts > 1 ether the stored betLimit != amount.

For any uint256 amount, when the owner calls AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the contract's betLimit equals the provided amount; the mutant clamps amounts > 1 ether to 1 ether so for some fuzzed amounts the stored betLimit != amount.

For any nonnegative amount provided to AdjustDifficulty by the owner, the reference contract accepts any new difficulty value (allowing decreases), while the mutant rejects attempts to set difficulty to a smaller value (requiring non-decrease), so there exists inputs where the call succeeds on the reference but reverts on the mutant.

For any owner-originated call to AdjustDifficulty(amount), the reference contract always allows changing difficulty to any uint256 (including decreases), while the mutant rejects attempts that lower difficulty; therefore the property: 'owner can successfully call AdjustDifficulty(amount) for all amount values' holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant for some inputs where amount < current difficulty.

For any uint256 amount and when called by the owner, the reference C permits AdjustDifficulty(amount) to complete (does not revert) for every amount, while the mutant sometimes reverts when amount is less than the current difficulty (it forbids decreasing difficulty).

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling AdjustDifficulty(amount) on the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) and results in difficulty being exactly amount; the mutant sometimes reverts when amount < current difficulty, so there exist owner calls where the reference accepts and sets difficulty but the mutant rejects them.

For any uint256 newDifficulty and when called by the owner, the reference contract always accepts AdjustDifficulty(newDifficulty) and sets difficulty to newDifficulty; the mutant sometimes refuses (reverts) when newDifficulty < current difficulty, so there exist owner inputs where the reference updates difficulty but the mutant does not.

After calling AdjustDifficulty(x) the contract's difficulty getter returns x (the new value) — reference always sets difficulty to the passed amount, while the mutant emits the event before updating state causing the emitted value to differ from the final difficulty for some inputs.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling AdjustDifficulty(amount) always results in the stored difficulty equaling the passed amount; the mutant still sets difficulty to amount but emits the old difficulty value in the event (so the emitted event value can differ from the final stored difficulty), which the test detects by observing that difficulty() equals the argument after the call.

For any owner caller and any uint256 newDifficulty, after calling AdjustDifficulty(newDifficulty) the contract's public difficulty() equals newDifficulty (the reference sets state to the passed value and emits that new value; the mutant emits the old value before updating, so the emitted event value can differ though the stored difficulty still equals the argument — to detect the mutant we check that calling AdjustDifficulty then querying difficulty() returns the passed value and that the call itself succeeds for all inputs).

For every owner caller and any uint256 amount, immediately after calling AdjustDifficulty(amount) the public getter difficulty() equals the passed amount; the mutant emits the old difficulty in the event before updating, which can cause observers who read the emitted event to see a value differing from the final stored difficulty (so the invariant that stored difficulty equals the argument after the call remains true for reference but can be observed as violated via emitted event ordering) — we test that difficulty() == amount always holds after the call.

For every caller who is the owner and for every uint256 newDifficulty, after calling AdjustDifficulty(newDifficulty) the contract's public difficulty() equals newDifficulty (reference satisfies this for all inputs; the mutant still sets difficulty but emits the old value before changing — while stored value equals newDifficulty, the emitted event differs from the new value, so observing via a try/catch on AdjustDifficulty still yields success but the mutant can be distinguished by comparing the post-call difficulty to the argument when the caller is not the owner; however to produce a failing case for the mutant we instead rely on the fact that onlyOwner prevents non-owners from calling AdjustDifficulty — the reference always reverts for non-owners while the mutant also reverts, so we fuzz an owner call and check stored value equals argument),

For all callers, only the contract owner can successfully call AdjustDifficulty on the reference; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner check allows non-owners to change difficulty, violating this property for some caller.

For any caller address x, only the contract owner (the deployer) can successfully change difficulty on the reference; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner check allows some non-owner caller (found by the fuzzer) to change difficulty, so there exists an input where AdjustDifficulty succeeds from a non-owner and thus changes c.currentDifficulty().

For every caller address, calling AdjustDifficulty on the correct contract reverts (only the owner can call it), so the public difficulty never changes when a non-owner calls it; the mutant removes the owner check allowing some non-owner input to succeed and change difficulty.

For any non-owner caller and any input amount, calling AdjustDifficulty should revert (so difficulty remains unchanged) on the reference contract, whereas the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller to successfully change difficulty.

For every caller address and difficulty value, when a non-owner attempts to call AdjustDifficulty on the reference contract the call reverts (difficulty stays as deployed), whereas the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller and value (found by the fuzzer) to succeed and change difficulty.

After the owner calls OpenToThePublic(), the contract's openToPublic flag must be true for every call by the owner (reference satisfies this; the mutant which sets it to false breaks this for some owner calls).

For any caller who is the contract owner, invoking OpenToThePublic() always sets c.currentDifficulty()/c.currentBetLimit() unaffected but more directly: invoking OpenToThePublic() when called by the owner flips the openToPublic flag to true (reference) — the mutant leaves it false; we observe this through behavior: after owner calls OpenToThePublic(), a subsequent wager() call by a non-owner real EOA should succeed only if openToPublic became true, so the reference allows a wager while the mutant blocks it.

For any EOA player and wager amount equal to the contract's bet limit, when the owner calls OpenToThePublic(), the contract must allow that player to call wager() (i.e., wager() does not revert); the mutant that sets openToPublic = false will block such a wager for some inputs, causing wager() to revert.

For any owner address, calling OpenToThePublic() makes the contract accept a subsequent wager() from a real EOA (i.e., wager() does not revert) when that wager matches the contract's bet limit; the mutant that sets openToPublic = false breaks this by causing such a wager to revert for some fuzzed player and betLimit inputs.

For every owner caller, invoking OpenToThePublic() results in the contract allowing any real EOA (tx.origin == msg.sender) to successfully call donate() (a payable public function that requires openToPublic) afterwards; the mutant that sets openToPublic = false breaks this because donate() will revert for some fuzzed donor addresses/amounts after the owner call.
For all callers, only the contract owner can set openToPublic to true by calling OpenToThePublic(); the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to make openToPublic true.

For every caller, only the contract owner can make openToPublic become true by calling OpenToThePublic(); the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows a non-owner caller to set openToPublic true, so there exists an input (a non-owner address) for which the mutant makes openToPublic true but the reference does not.

For every caller address, only the contract owner can successfully set openToPublic to true by calling OpenToThePublic(); the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to make openToPublic true, so there exists a caller for which the mutant yields openToPublic == true while the reference keeps it false.

For every caller address, calling OpenToThePublic() on the correct contract reverts for non-owners (so openToPublic remains false), whereas the mutant allows at least one non-owner caller to set openToPublic true; equivalently: only the owner can successfully complete OpenToThePublic() on the reference, so a non-owner caller cannot make address(c).balance or other state-change-observable effects — the mutant breaks this by letting some non-owner call succeed.

For every caller address, on the reference contract only the owner can successfully set openToPublic true via OpenToThePublic(); the mutant (which removes the onlyOwner guard) allows some non-owner caller to successfully call OpenToThePublic() and make openToPublic true.

Calling OpenToThePublic always sets openToPublic to true (idempotently enabling public) in the reference contract for any initial state; the mutant that toggles it will, for some initial states, leave openToPublic false after the call, violating this rule.

Calling OpenToThePublic() by the owner always results in openToPublic being true in the reference, whereas the mutant that toggles can leave it false for some initial states; therefore for any initial openToPublic value, after calling OpenToThePublic() the reference yields openToPublic == true, but the mutant yields false for at least one initial state.

For any initial state and any owner caller, calling OpenToThePublic() results in openToPublic == true in the reference; the mutant that toggles can leave it false for some initial states, so there exist inputs (initial state plus call) where the mutant violates this.

For any caller who is the owner, calling OpenToThePublic() always results in c.openToPublic() becoming true in the reference implementation; the mutant that toggles can leave it false for some initial states (so the property can be violated).

For any initial boolean state X and when called by the owner, invoking OpenToThePublic() on the reference contract always results in openToPublic == true; the mutant that toggles may leave openToPublic == false for some initial X, so there exist inputs where the mutant violates this.

For any owner-supplied amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) sets c.currentBetLimit() equal to the exact amount provided; the mutant that adds +1 breaks this by making currentBetLimit() == amount + 1 for some inputs.

For any uint256 amount passed by the owner to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference contract sets currentBetLimit() equal to that amount; the mutant sets it to amount+1 for some inputs, so there exists an amount where currentBetLimit() != amount (the mutant violates equality).

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, after calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the contract's currentBetLimit() equals the provided amount; the mutant that adds +1 will for some fuzzed amount produce currentBetLimit() != amount, violating this property.

For every owner address and any wager limit value, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) from the owner results in currentBetLimit() - amount == 0; the mutant increments stored betLimit by 1 so there exist fuzzed amounts where currentBetLimit() - amount == 1, violating this invariant.

For any uint256 amount and when called by the owner, AdjustBetAmounts(amount) results in c.currentBetLimit() being equal to the provided amount; the mutant that sets betLimit = amount + 1 will cause c.currentBetLimit() != amount for some fuzzed amounts.

For any owner caller and any amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on the correct contract updates the public betLimit to equal the provided amount; the mutant emits the event but leaves betLimit unchanged, so for some fuzzed amount the post-call betLimit will differ.

For any uint256 amount and when called by the owner, AdjustBetAmounts(amount) updates the contract's public betLimit to that amount; the mutant emits an event but fails to update betLimit, so for some fuzzed amounts the post-call betLimit will differ.

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, after calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the public getter currentBetLimit() equals the provided amount in the reference but the mutant (which never assigns betLimit) can leave currentBetLimit() unchanged for some amounts, so the property is: calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) by the owner makes currentBetLimit() == amount.

For any caller who is the owner, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) always makes the contract's winnersPot() (which equals half the contract balance) remain unaffected by emitted events — specifically, after owner calls AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the public currentBetLimit() increases or decreases to match amount and winnersPot() remains equal to address(c).balance/2; the mutant fails to update betLimit so there exist amounts where currentBetLimit() != amount (detected via getter), thus violating the rule.
